title: Activation of Intradental Neurons in Mice via Electrical Stimulation
author: Wan, Ronan, et al.
materials: Standard Ear Bars and Rubber Tips

steps.title: Gather components and 3D‑print nosecone
steps.instruction: Acquire all commercial parts listed in Table S1. 3D‑print the main nosecone body and the adjustable nose isosleeve using resin stereolithography (SLA, MSLA, or DLP). Orient the main body front‑side‑up and the isosleeve front‑side‑down, set a 5 mm build‑platform elevation, generate supports only from the platform, and use a 5 µm layer thickness; adjust other printer and resin settings as needed.

steps.title: Assemble nosecone sliding mechanism
steps.instruction: Hook the sliding block on one side of the isosleeve into the corresponding groove on the main nosecone body, then gently push the isosleeve upward until both sliding blocks are constrained by the grooves. Test forward‑backward sliding; if the blocks are oversized, reduce layer exposure time and compensate for resin shrinkage before re‑printing.

steps.title: Print palate mounting tip components
steps.instruction: 3D‑print the three palate‑mounting‑tip subcomponents (main body, nosecone guide slot, and M3 thumbscrew adapter) using a filament‑based printer (FDM/FFF) for easier post‑processing and material compatibility.

steps.title: Build palate mounting bar assembly
steps.instruction: Assemble the palate mounting bar as follows:

substeps.instruction: Insert three M3 × 4 mm knurled nuts into the main palate‑mounting‑tip body using a soldering iron.
Attach M3 thumbscrew adapters to one M3 × 12 mm and one M3 × 18 mm socket‑head cap screw; apply super glue to bond adapters to screws.
Secure the nosecone guide slot to the custom nosecone with an M3 × 14 mm screw (hole is unthreaded; tap gently).
Attach the custom nosecone and guide slot to the main palate‑mounting‑tip body with the M3 × 12 mm thumbscrew (optional M3 washer between screw and slot).
Place a 0.4 × 5 × 10 mm compression spring (7 laps) between the nosecone and palate tip; thread the M3 × 18 mm thumbscrew through the spring and tighten slightly (optional washer).
Insert an MS3R optical post into the palate tip body and lock it with an M3 × 10 mm socket‑head cap screw.

steps.title: Connect nosecone to anesthesia system
steps.instruction: Attach standard tubing to the inlet and outlet barbs of the custom nosecone, following the arrow markings to distinguish inspiration from expiration channels; ensure all connections are secure to maintain stable isoflurane delivery.

steps.title: Assemble custom stereotaxic stage
steps.instruction: Construct the stereotaxic platform as follows:

substeps.instruction: Connect the top platform to the goniometer using the provided thread adapters.
Secure the bottom platform to the goniometer with M6 × 10 mm socket‑head cap screws.
Mount optical posts, post clamps, stereotaxic ear bars, and the palate‑mounting‑bar assembly onto the top platform; adjust positions for the specific mouse size.
Tighten all clamps and adapters firmly to prevent motion.
Verify that the assembled setup provides unobstructed optical and physical access to the oral cavity, with the mouse mandible hanging over the platform edge for better accessibility.

steps.title: Fabricate grounded incisor retractor
steps.instruction: Create the incisor retractor (cathode) as follows:

substeps.instruction: Bend a 1 mm‑diameter stainless‑steel spring wire into the configuration shown in Figures 2A‑B using pliers.
Solder a sufficiently long 22 AWG wire to the retractor; apply stainless‑steel soldering flux to avoid cold joints.
Expose 5 mm of the conductor at the opposite end; optionally tin the exposed conductor.
Measure resistance between the alligator clip and the top and bottom hooks with a multimeter; ensure resistance ≤ 5 Ω and re‑solder if higher.

steps.title: Print buccal retractor
steps.instruction: 3D‑print the buccal retractor using a non‑brittle, durable material; filament‑based FDM/FFF printing is recommended for durability and material compatibility.

steps.title: Construct electrical stimulator
steps.instruction: Build the anode stimulator for delivering pulses to a molar:

substeps.instruction: Solder a sufficiently long 22 AWG silicone wire to the metallic region of a 040 × 31 mm dental file near its base; expose 5 mm of the conductor at the opposite end and optionally tin it.
Measure resistance between the wire end and the stimulator tip; ensure resistance ≤ 5 Ω and re‑solder if necessary.

Insulate the metallic region of the dental file, leaving a 2 mm tip uninsulated.  Alternatively, use a ~0.2 mm stainless‑steel spring wire and cover with 2:1‑ratio miniature heat‑shrink tubing (inner diameter < 0.4 mm after shrinkage).
Gently bend the file 1.5 mm from its tip by approximately 70°.

description: Tooth sensation and pain are mediated by trigeminal sensory neurons that innervate the tooth’s inner pulp and dentin (intradental neurons).1,2,3,4 As projections of intradental neurons terminate beneath the tooth’s hard enamel, non-invasive and precise methods to achieve their activation are technically challenging. This protocol describes a procedure to selectively and repeatably activate intradental neurons using controlled electrical stimulation without inducing tooth damage, as validated by in vivo trigeminal calcium imaging in Ronan et al.1 The approach enables targeted neuronal activation while maintaining the structural integrity of the tooth and can also be applied in the context of pulpitis or tooth disease models. In this protocol, we first describe the preparation of a custom stereotaxic stage and the fabrication of custom incisor and buccal retractors. These steps provide sufficient optical and physical access to the oral cavity and mouse molar teeth in anesthetized, head-fixed mice. Next, we describe how to construct a custom electrical stimulator setup to administer electric pulse to an individual molar. Finally, we provide instructions to combine the use of these approaches to achieve targeted activation of intradental neurons. These procedures provide a flexible method for repeatable activation of intradental neurons without inducing tooth mechanical damage. They are also applicable to functional studies of intradental neurons in the context of pulpitis or diseases compromising tooth integrity.
